Porcupine Spotted in Vermont Looks Like a Snowball With Quills and the Reason Behind the Rare Look Is Simpler Than Expected A wild animal has been making headlines in Vermont, and it's not just any common animal. It's a rare albino porcupine!
 The porcupine was spotted crossing a road in North Pomfret in mid-October, and its creamy white fur has the whole Internet talking. Videos of the animal encounter have been making rounds on news outlets like NBC 10 Boston, but none have explained what causes albinism or just how rare this fur color mutation is.
 That's a once-in-a-lifetime animal sighting, and the person behind the camera was incredibly lucky to be in the right place at the right time. If you ask some of the excited video viewers who commented on @nbc10boston 's video, however, they'll say they're the lucky ones!
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "I lived in Vermont my entire life, and never heard of a town called North Pomfret, nor have I seen a porcupine that cute!" wrote @tkdgirl1993. She tagged Vermont Fish and Wildlife, urging them to "protect that albino porcupine at all costs!"
 Related: Viewers Were Shocked When Mama Porcupine Ran Off Without Her Adorable Baby 
 Another commenter had a similar thought, writing, "What a cutie. I'm not sure how I feel about the exact location being shared here. There are too many cruel people."
 Occasionally, unique animals like Jimothy the raccoon or this albino porcupine become targets for hunters, especially if they go viral. While I hope no one goes looking for the all-white porcupine to begin with, I'm glad it wandered back into the forest where it can stay hidden indefinitely.
 What Causes Albinism in Animals?
 Only one in 10,000 baby porcupines is born albino, making porcupines like the one in this video especially rare. But what exactly is albinism?
 Advertisement Advertisement 🐶   SIGN UP to get "pawsitivity" delivered right to your inbox with inspiring & entertaining stories about our furry & feathered friends 🐾🐾 
 Albinism is a genetic mutation that occurs when the cells that control an animal's fur and eye color are unable to produce melanin, the pigment that gives fur its color. Animals can be pure albino, like the all-white porcupine in this video, or they can have leucism, which results in normal fur patterns in lighter colors instead. Animals with pure albinism will also have pink or red eyes.
 Knowing more about albinism makes this rare wild animal even more special in my eyes. I'm so grateful that the person who spotted it shared the video with the world, because most of us will never see a porcupine, let alone an albino one, ourselves.
